source_text: Deinde, ut praerupta opinionis tuae sequamur, argumentaris tali conditione liberum arbitrium ordinatum fuisse, ut vim suam merito secutae voluntatis amitteret, et qualitatis quam elegisset necessitatem, in reliquum sustineret. Hinc ergo quid a nobis referatur attende. Siccine putas hominem creatum, ut hanc electae qualitatis necessitatem in utraque parte pateretur, id est, ut si bonum voluisset, ulterius peccare non posset; et si elegisset malum, ultra se emendare nequiret? An ut tantummodo malam partem mali necessitas sequeretur, in bona autem nihil tale contingeret, sed semper periculis varietatum pateret? Ex his duobus quodlibet sumito: si dixeris talem factam esse naturam, quae mali tantum necessitatem pateretur; nulli dubium remanebit, teterrimam eam definiri, cui peioris partis violentia sola tribuatur; probaturque Adam quoque malae fuisse naturae; et nullius remanebit voluntarii, sub qua delitescas, umbra commissi. Sin autem profitearis, etiam in boni parte idem fuisse secuturum, id est, ut si bonum voluisset, ulterius peccare non posset; refero: Cur ergo peccavit? Cur nullam passus est boni necessitatem, ut insidiis diaboli impenetrabilis appareret, qui aliquo tempore, priusquam peccaret, fuisse obediens Deo invenitur? Neque enim illico quod ingressu animae limus intepuit, in appetitum malae voluntatis exarsit. Legitur quinimmo, ad culturam paradisi custodiamque translatus accepisse praeceptum a Deo, ut universis fructibus vesceretur, sed a ligno scientiae boni et mali, dicto audiens abstineret. Antequam ergo de latere eius corpus formaretur uxoris, obediens mansit imperio, amoeni ruris cultor innocuus; post hoc vero, adiutorium similis sibi consortis emeruit. Inculcavit nempe has distinctiones temporum Scripturae fides. Postquam vero iam sibi mulierem vidit paratam, in tantum praecepto Dei sedulo famulabatur officio, ut etiam feminae legem, quam acceperat, intimaret. Non solum igitur custos divini, sed etiam praedicator imperii, condocefecit Eva et reverentiam praecipientis, et genus servitutis, et causam timoris. Inde est quippe quod etiam mulier congredienti diabolo obluctata sollicite, cui nihil Deus imperaverat, refellit serpentis prima fronte mendacia, et dicit non abstinentiam omnium lignorum, sicut ille confinxerat, sed cum permissu fertilitatis universae unius tantum mandatam arbusculae cautionem, metumque mortis obiectum, qui praevaricatores iure sequeretur. Non ergo brevi tempore apparet Adam custodisse mandatum; sed etiam Evam curam devotionis habuisse, quae scientiae et divinitatis amore collapsa est. Cur ergo illa iustitia, illa devotio, quae in Adam diu, in Eva aliquandiu viguit, non eripuit delinquendi possibilitatem, ut boni necessitas impenetrabiles eos suadelis sontibus exhiberet? Fuerunt ergo quamdiu voluerunt obedientes, nec tamen perdiderunt merito devotionis facultatem praevaricandi; denique lapsi sunt [n38] ; igitur et posteaquam peccaverunt, manifestum est nequaquam eos potuisse vim correctionis amittere. Et ideo ut in omnibus locis, hic quoque totum quod confinxeras perdidisti; quia peccatum illud primorum hominum nec ullorum fecit criminum necessitatem, nec transiit in naturam; sicut iustitia quae praecessit, nec virtutum intulit necessitatem, nec sibi vias seminum vindicavit.
pass_a_gloss: Then, that we may follow the cliffs of your opinion, you argue that free decision was ordained by such a condition, that it would lose its force by the desert of the following will, and would sustain for the rest a necessity of the quality which it had chosen. From here therefore attend what is reported by us. Do you so think the human created, that he would suffer this necessity of a chosen quality on each side, that is, that if he had willed good, he could not further sin; and if he had chosen evil, he would be unable further to amend himself? Or that a necessity of evil would follow only the evil part, but on the good nothing of such a kind would happen, but it would always lie open to the dangers of varieties? From these two take whichever you will: if you shall have said that such a nature was made, which would suffer a necessity of evil only; it will remain doubtful to none that it is defined most foul, to which the violence of the worse part alone is attributed; and Adam also is proved to have been of an evil nature; and no shadow of a voluntary thing committed, under which you may hide, will remain. But if you profess that even on the side of good the same would have followed, that is, that if he had willed good, he could not further sin; I report: Why therefore did he sin? Why did he suffer no necessity of good, so that he would appear impenetrable to the devil's snares, who is found at some time, before he sinned, to have been obedient to God? For not immediately when the mud grew warm by the entrance of a soul did he burn into an appetite of an evil will. It is read on the contrary that transferred to the culture and custody of paradise he received a precept from God, that he would feed on all fruits, but hearing the word would abstain from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Before therefore from his side the body of a wife was formed, he remained obedient to the command, an innocent cultivator of a pleasant countryside; but after this he earned the help of a partner like himself. The faith of Scripture indeed impressed these distinctions of times. But after he already saw a woman prepared for himself, he was serving the precept of God with so diligent an office that he even intimated to the woman the law which he had received. Not only therefore a guardian of the divine, but even a preacher of the command, he thoroughly taught Eve both the reverence of the one precepting, and the kind of servitude, and the cause of fear. From there it is indeed that even the woman, having struggled anxiously with the approaching devil, to whom God had commanded nothing, refutes on the first face the serpent's lies, and says not an abstinence of all trees, as he had feigned, but with a permission of universal fertility a caution of one little tree only mandated, and a fear of death objected, which would by right follow prevaricators. Not therefore by a brief time does Adam appear to have kept the mandate; but even Eve to have had a care of devotion, who collapsed by a love of knowledge and of divinity. Why therefore did that justice, that devotion, which thrived in Adam long, in Eve for some time, not snatch away a possibility of offending, so that a necessity of good would exhibit them impenetrable to guilty persuasions? They were therefore obedient as long as they willed, nor nevertheless did they lose by the desert of devotion a faculty of prevaricating; finally they fell; therefore even after they sinned, it is manifest that they could by no means have lost the force of correction. And therefore as in all places, here also you lost the whole which you had feigned; because that sin of the first humans neither made a necessity of any charges, nor passed into nature; as the justice which preceded neither brought a necessity of virtues, nor claimed for itself the ways of seeds.

pass_b_english: Next, to follow the precipices of your opinion, you argue that free will was arranged on this condition: it would lose its power as the consequence of the will that followed, and thereafter endure the necessity of the quality it chose. Attend, then, to our reply. Do you think humanity was created to suffer this necessity of the chosen quality on both sides? If someone willed good, could he thereafter not sin; and if he chose evil, could he no longer reform? Or would necessity of evil follow only the evil choice, while nothing similar happened on the good side, which would always remain exposed to the dangers of change?

Take whichever of these alternatives you please. If you say nature was made to suffer only the necessity of evil, no one will doubt that a nature assigned compulsion solely toward the worse side is being defined as utterly repulsive. Adam too is proved to have possessed an evil nature, and no shadow of a voluntary offense will remain for you to hide beneath.

But if you profess that the same consequence would have followed on goodness’s side—if he had willed good he could no longer sin—I reply: Why, then, did he sin? Why did no necessity of good make him impervious to the devil’s plots, when he is found to have obeyed God for some time before sinning? The instant the clay grew warm with the soul’s entrance, he did not immediately blaze into the desire of an evil will. Rather, we read that he was placed in paradise to cultivate and guard it and received God’s command to eat all its fruits but obediently abstain from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

Before his wife’s body was formed from his side, he therefore remained obedient to the command, an innocent cultivator of that delightful countryside. Afterward he received the help of a companion like himself. Scripture’s truthful account emphasizes these distinctions of time. Once he saw the woman prepared for him, he served God’s command with such diligent devotion that he also informed her of the law he had received. Thus he not only kept but also proclaimed the divine command, teaching Eve reverence for the one commanding, the kind of obedience required, and the reason for fear.

That is why the woman, to whom God had given no command, resisted the devil’s approach attentively. At first she refuted the serpent’s lies. She said abstinence from all trees had not been commanded, as he invented; rather, permission to enjoy all their fruit came with a warning about just one little tree, and the fear of death was set before them as the rightful consequence for transgressors. It therefore appears that Adam kept the command for no short time. Eve too cared about devotion, although she fell through love of knowledge and divinity.

Why, then, did the justice and devotion that flourished a long time in Adam and for some time in Eve not remove their ability to do wrong, so that a necessity of good made them impervious to guilty persuasions? They were obedient for as long as they wished, yet the merit of their devotion did not cost them their ability to transgress: in the end they fell (Genesis 2–3). Therefore, even after sinning, it is clear that they could not have lost the power to reform. Here, as everywhere, you have lost everything you invented. That sin of the first humans neither created necessity for any crimes nor passed into nature, just as their previous justice neither imposed necessity for virtues nor claimed the pathways of reproductive seed (Genesis 2:7) (Genesis 2:15–17) (Genesis 2:18–23) (Genesis 3:1–6).

choices.why: Glossary default: arbitrium is the decision-power, not a later Augustinian/Reformation free-will locus.
Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Freedom to abstain is required for will and sin.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.
